name: American Folk Vernacular

description.short: Log, shotgun, farmhouse, and the other unstyled house types that most Americans actually lived in.
description.long:
Most American houses were never designed and never carried a style name. They were built from types — a log pen, a double pen, a shotgun, a gable-front-and-wing farmhouse — that encode generations of accumulated judgment about span, heating, ventilation, and how a family grows.

Treating this family as residual would be a mistake. These types are the substrate the styled architecture sits on, they are the direct ancestors of the current market's most popular idiom, and their expansion logic — how a house grows without breaking — is the property that formal styles most conspicuously lack and that a generative design system most needs.

defining_characteristics: Type rather than style as the unit of design
Structural and climatic logic governing form directly
Ornament minimal, applied late, and bought rather than made
Expansion and accretion as designed-in properties
Transmission entirely by craft memory and imitation
